newsitem.title: PERU: Peru negotiator and rebels to meet again on hostages.
newsitem.headline: Peru negotiator and rebels to meet again on hostages.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima were to meet a Peruvian government negotiator again on Saturday to try to draft an agenda for talks to end the 60-day siege without bloodshed.

The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) and President Alberto Fujimori's negotiator Domingo Palermo met on Friday in a Red Cross safe house opposite the residence to swap lists of items they want discussed in negotiations.

Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent, part of a guarantors commission mediating the talks, told reporters outside: "The guarantors and observers consider the conversations have resulted in real progress. The conversations will continue tomorrow."
But he added: "So far, the agenda has not been agreed."

Other guarantors for the talks are the Vatican, the Red Cross and an observer from Japan. This week has seen a breakthrough in the standoff in a leafy suburb of Peru's capital that began on Dec. 17 when 15 heavily armed MRTA rebels led by Nestor Cerpa Cartolini stormed a cocktail party, taking hundreds of hostages.

They released most of them but kept 72 including Fujimori's brother Pedro, two cabinet ministers, top security officials and judges, the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivian and about two dozen Japanese businessmen.

As the days and weeks pass, worries about the physical and mental strains on the mostly middle-aged hostages increase. The Red Cross says none is seriously ill but many are being treated for hypertension, digestive problems and depression. Doctors allowed in to treat them say some are jogging and dieting to cope with two months' captivity.

They have spent Christmas, New Year's Day and now Valentine's Day away from their families. Wives and girlfriends gave the Red Cross boxes of chocolates and other Valentine's gifts for them on Friday and 72 couples married at a mass ceremony nearby to show solidarity with the hostages.

The deans of the country's law colleges, dressed in their legal silks, held a rally outside the besieged residence on Friday in solidarity with the men "who have been victims of the violation of their most fundamental rights."
"This unexpected episode must be ended quickly guaranteeing the physical integrity and lives of the hostages," Vladimir Paz de Barra, head of Lima's Law College, said.

The MRTA rebels are demanding the release of 400 comrades from Peruvian jails in exchange for the hostages' lives -- a condition that Fujimori, supported by world leaders including U.S. President Bill Clinton, refuses to consider.

The meeting on Friday between Palermo and Cerpa Cartolini's lieutenant Rolly Rojas was the second since Tuesday when the two sides ended weeks of deadlock and restarted face-to-face talks broken off on Dec. 28.

In Tokyo, where the Japanese government and media have been following the crisis closely, the Foreign Ministry criticised Japanese TV Asahi's Tsuyoshi Hitomi, who left a radio transmitter in the residence when he sneaked in last month to meet the rebels. It said he could have put the hostage talks at risk.
TV Asahi staff made radio contact with 10 Japanese hostages in late January and conveyed their messages to their families, but the network says it did not broadcast the radio contact.

"We have repeatedly conveyed our concern to TV Asahi that, depending on the way the radio was used, it could have grave impact on the course of talks between the Peruvian government and the MRTA," the ministry said in a statement.
At an Asian and European foreign ministers meeting in Singapore on Friday participants expressed support for Peru and Japan in the crisis and condemned the MRTA for its "criminal act."
